prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: [val] Co-bottleneck · Framework trade-offs (language en).
Grid: 4 columns × 4 rows. Row headers: none declared.
Per-column content facts (content px at 13px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "Option" · longest unbreakable word 59px · one-line width 102px
  col 2: header "Strengths" · longest unbreakable word 72px · one-line width 541px
  col 3: header "Weaknesses" · longest unbreakable word 79px · one-line width 646px
  col 4: header "Verdict" · longest unbreakable word 46px · one-line width 46px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 582px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 581px.
Fixed: content, font, 13px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 582px (different strategies, not small variations).
Reply ONLY JSON: {"understanding":{"purpose":"","reading":"","groups":["columns that belong together and why"],"keep_intact":[""],"may_wrap":[""]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[int px per column, column 1 first],"idea":"one sentence"}]}

log.raw: {"understanding":{"purpose":"Compare framework options by their strengths, weaknesses, and overall verdict.","reading":"Readers scan the option names, then compare the paired strengths and weaknesses before checking each verdict. Each row should remain easy to follow across the table.","groups":["Strengths and Weaknesses are parallel explanatory columns and should have enough space for readable phrases.","Option and Verdict frame each comparison: one identifies the choice and the other gives its assessment."],"keep_intact":["Individual words and the short verdicts.","Option names where practical, especially when existing row height can accommodate a natural wrap."],"may_wrap":["Strengths and weaknesses can wrap at word boundaries.","Multiword option names can wrap at word boundaries."]},"designs":[{"name":"A","widths":[105,190,206,80],"idea":"Give the paired explanation columns most of the width, with slightly more for the longer weaknesses and compact framing columns."},{"name":"B","widths":[125,165,180,111],"idea":"Give option names and verdicts more room for scanning while allowing the explanations to form deeper text blocks."},{"name":"C","widths":[85,210,216,70],"idea":"Maximize space for side-by-side comparison of strengths and weaknesses, accepting wrapped option names and a tight verdict column."}]}
